notes:
I've grouped the notes by verse, with the source URL after each point. Searches were limited, so a few areas are thin or missing, and I list those at the end.

**A note on the whole chapter (vv. 1–3)**
- The commentators disagree about who is speaking in vv. 1–3. Ellicott says the prophet puts words of imperfect penitence in the lips of those in trouble who count too soon on God's compassion; they are not an exhortation to repentance, for they are followed by indignant expostulation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/6.htm
- Enduring Word reads them the other way: Hosea prays with the right heart in response to God's chastening. Instead of arguing with God or resenting His correction, he leads Israel in humble prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-6/
- Gill finds both groups in the chapter: some who were truly penitent and stirred up one another to return to the Lord, and others who had only a form of religion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/geb/hosea-6.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says these verses were improperly torn from the preceding chapter, to which they naturally belong. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/6-1.htm

**v. 1**
- Pulpit: the words show strong faith and firm confidence: He who tore will also heal. It says God is pictured tearing as a lion tears its prey, yet the speakers show no resentment, only submission and acknowledgment that the punishment is just. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-6.html
- Precept Austin: "return" means to repent, a change of heart that results in a change of direction. In its dispensational reading, Israel in Hosea's day did not return, and the call awaits a future fulfilment when the nation repents and is saved in Christ at His Second Coming. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-6-commentary
- Spurgeon (Baptist), quoted by Precept Austin, applies the verse to the troubled sinner: God alone can heal and delights to do it, since binding up the broken-hearted is the Lord's office. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-6-commentary
- Gill (Baptist) also applies it to Christ, saying the great Physician heals them by his stripes and wounds, by the application of his blood, by means of his word. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/6-1.html

**v. 2: the main debated verse ("the third day")**
- **Reading 1: a short time.** Ellicott takes "after two days" as tomorrow and "the third day" as after a short time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/6.htm The NET translation renders it the same way: "He will restore us in a very short time; he will heal us in a little while." https://www.blueletterbible.org/sample/net/hos/6/1/
- **Reading 2: Christ's resurrection.** Ellicott notes that Jerome, Luther and Pusey see sole reference to Christ's resurrection. Ellicott, siding with Calvin and others, calls this "far-fetched over-refinement" with no New Testament authority. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/6.htm This means the Lutheran tradition (Luther) and the Reformed tradition (Calvin) part ways here, at least as Ellicott reports it.
- **Calvin himself takes a middle path.** He notes the verse is usually referred to Christ: God would raise up his Church, for Christ did not rise privately for himself but for his members. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_hosea/hosea_6_2.htm He also uses it pastorally: when God seems to delay, flee to Christ, whose resurrection is a mirror of our life, for he lay in the tomb to the third day. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom26.xiii.iii.html
- **Barnes and Pusey: strongly about Christ.** Barnes says the resurrection of Christ, and ours in Him, "could not be more plainly foretold." Pusey adds that the ten tribes were never restored, the return from Babylon was a mere shadow, and the days have nothing in history to match them except Christ rising on the third day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/6-2.htm ; https://biblehub.com/sermons/hosea/6-2.htm
- **Both readings at once.** Matthew Henry reads it as national deliverance but says it "seems to have a further reference to the resurrection of Jesus Christ." Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls it Israel's revival in type, antitypically referring in full accuracy only to Messiah, the ideal Israel. Benson calls it a short time of national restoration with "an oblique, allusion to our Lord's resurrection". All three are on https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/6-2.htm
- **Enduring Word (on your Pentecostal/charismatic list):** a shadowy prophecy of Jesus' resurrection on the third day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-6/
- **Gill's millennium idea.** Gill applies the verse to the future conversion of the Jews. He suggests, explicitly "only as a conjecture", that the "two days" are two thousand years counted from the Roman destruction. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/6-2.html
- **Church Fathers.** Barnes notes the ancient fathers generally understood these words of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/6-2.htm A Bible Hub Q&A page lists Justin Martyr and Tertullian as citing the verse for the resurrection. https://biblehub.com/q/Hosea_6_2_s_link_to_Jesus_resurrection.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit translates the opening "Then let us know, follow on to know, Jehovah," and links it to Hosea 4:1, where Jehovah had become unknown in Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-6.html
- Enduring Word links it to Hosea 4:6 ("destroyed for lack of knowledge"). It says knowing God must be more than superficial, a real pursuit, and God reveals Himself especially through His word. It explains the rain image: in Israel, rain was the only way crops were watered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-6/
- Matthew Henry: God's grace in Christ is both the latter and the former rain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/6-2.htm
- **Debated modern movement.** Enduring Word notes that this verse, with Deuteronomy 11:14 and Joel 2:23, gave the name of the "Latter Rain Movement" starting in 1948. It lists that movement's distinctives, including the "five-fold ministry" and restoration of apostles and prophets, replacement theology and dominion theology. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-6/

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: here God's reply begins, lamenting how short-lived their repentance is. "Goodness" is better rendered "love." It is like a morning cloud which promises rain and does not give it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/6.htm
- Gill gives historical examples: reforms under Jehu in Israel, and under Hezekiah and Josiah in Judah, that did not go on, nor last long. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/geb/hosea-6.html
- Pulpit applies it to people today: some visited in illness vow to live differently, yet with returning health comes returning indifference. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-6.html

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: the Greek Old Testament (LXX) reads "I have mowed down their prophets," but that would break the parallel with "words of my mouth." The sense is "I have slain them by the announcement of deserved doom." He thinks a copying error crept into the Hebrew text and translates the last line "My judgment shall go forth as the light". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/6.htm
- Pulpit: because their religion was shallow and formal, God cut them down through his prophets by fierce denunciations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-6.html
- Spurgeon, as summarised by Precept Austin, describes God as a "rough hewer," using convicting words and painful providences to cut away self-righteousness and false security. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-6-commentary

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: "mercy" is better rendered "love." Jesus took up this teaching in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7, and the moral ranks above the ceremonial. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/6.htm
- **"Not" means "rather than."** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Poole, Benson and the Cambridge Bible all say the "not" is comparative. God instituted sacrifice himself, so the point is that he values moral obedience more, not that he rejects sacrifice outright. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/6-6.htm
- **What "knowledge of God" means.** Gill takes it as knowing God in Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/6-6.html Benson calls it a supernatural gift through the influence of his enlightening Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/6-6.htm Pulpit calls it a sympathetic experience, not a scientific acquaintance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-6.html
- Enduring Word: Israel brought animals but never brought themselves as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-6/

**v. 7: a translation and theology debate**
- **Three possible readings.** NET notes: the Hebrew can mean (1) the man Adam, (2) "[sinful] men" in general, or (3) the town of Adam in the Jordan Valley (Joshua 3:16). Option 3 requires a small change to the Hebrew, prompted by the word "there." "The English versions are divided." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Hos&chapter=6&verse=7
- **Reformed: the covenant of works.** Thomas Boston preached this verse as the breach of the covenant of works. https://biblehub.com/sermons/hosea/6-7.htm Ligonier says commentators differ, but if it means the first man, it hints that the Mosaic covenant has some relationship to the covenant of works not shared by the other covenants. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/adam-and-israel
- **Baptist (Gill).** Gill lists the covenant of works in paradise among several options. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/6-7.html
- **Calvin disagrees with that reading.** He calls the "like Adam" explanation "frigid and diluted". https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/6-7.html
- **Matthew Henry:** as Adam transgressed the covenant of innocency, Israel transgressed the covenant of grace, there in Canaan, another paradise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/6-7.html
- **Dispensational (Constable):** the covenant Adam broke was the Adamic Covenant (Genesis 2:16-17), not the Mosaic covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/6-7.html
- **Lutheran and Catholic Latin tradition.** Pulpit prefers "like Adam," a rendering it says is supported by the Vulgate, Cyril, Luther. https://biblehub.com/hosea/6-7.htm
- **Against a covenant with Adam.** The Cambridge Bible objects that Genesis says nothing of a 'covenant' with Adam. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/6-7.htm
- **Catholic translations differ.** The Douay-Rheims has "like Adam," while the New American Bible has "at Adam". https://biblehub.com/hosea/6-7.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: "polluted" is more accurately "foot-tracked with blood." Gilead was a town east of the Jordan, and murder in a "city of refuge" adds to the horror. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/6.htm
- Pulpit: probably Ramoth-gilead, one of the cities of refuge Moses appointed. A place God ordained for good had been corrupted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-6.html

**v. 9**
- Ellicott translates: "the company of priests murder on the road to Shechem; yea, they execute the plot." Shechem was a city of refuge and a Levitical city on the road to Bethel, where the priests of the calf-idols lived. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/6.htm
- Pulpit: "Like priest, like people." A corrupted pulpit is the worst of all ministries. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-6.html

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: the "horrible thing" refers to polluting idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/6.htm
- Gill: the calf-idols at Dan and Bethel, set up by Jeroboam of Ephraim. He says both corporeal and spiritual whoredom, or idolatry, are here meant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/geb/hosea-6.html

**v. 11**
- **A harvest of judgment.** Ellicott: it is not of joy, but of sorrow and affliction, befalling Judah, like Israel, for her sins. He joins the last clause to chapter 7 and says the full turning of the captivity cannot be realised till Ephraim and Judah accept the Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/6.htm Pulpit agrees that Judah cannot escape reaping "a harvest" of wrath. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-6.html
- **A harvest of returning exiles.** Enduring Word: after the Babylonian exile the returnees settled mainly in Judah, so the harvest of returned exiles was mainly for Judah, not for Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-6/

**What I couldn't find**
- **Catholic and Orthodox sites:** I found nothing on newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The Catholic points above come only from translations and from Barnes's and Pulpit's mentions of the Fathers and the Vulgate.
- **Other modern scholarship:** nothing from bibleodyssey.org, and NET notes only for v. 7.
- **Methodist, Wesleyan and Lutheran writers on their own sites:** none found.
- **Prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching:** none found for this chapter. The Latter Rain note on v. 3 is the only debated modern movement that came up.
